newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican Indians stage forum, but without rebels.
newsitem.headline: Mexican Indians stage forum, but without rebels.

text.p: Mexican Indians representing 25 groups launched a controversial forum on Tuesday demanding political and social reforms, but the star guests -- Mexico's masked Zapatista rebels, did not attend.

As the Mayan Indian guerrillas in southeastern Mexico were bogged down in talks with peace mediators on whether they should be allowed safe travel to Mexico City to attend the forum, it opened demanding reform, but not revolution.

"Mexico needs change with strong intelligence and autonomy, but still not a revolution," said speaker Juan Simbo as he inaugurated the four-day National Indian Congress amid drums and traditional music.

In front of some 1,000 delegates, speakers voiced support for the Zapatistas, who are in a tense standoff in Chiapas state with the government that says they have no right to roam the country until they give up their arms and strip off their trademark ski-masks.
But the forum participants said their demands were not limited to success in the Indian rebel struggle in Chiapas.
"We don't want war but we do want a dignified peace, we want a united Mexico, a Mexico where there is no corruption," said Felix Sardan, another representative.

There are some eight million Indians from 96 ethnic groups in Mexico and more than half are unemployed and live in dire poverty, according to statistics from the National Indigenous Institute published in Reforma newspaper on Tuesday.

The plight of Mexico's downtrodden Indian communities was thrown under the world spotlight in January 1994, when mostly Indian fighters of the Zapatista National Liberation Army rose up in Chiapas demanding democracy and native rights. There was little fighting and the rebels have since been passively holed up in Chiapas.

The invitation to Zapatista leaders to make their first trip out of the state and go to Mexico City threw the government on the defensive, and it has threatened to arrest rebel leaders if they leave their jungle hideouts.
Late on Tuesday, reporters at a remote rebel base near the Guatemalan border said talks between rebel leaders and peace mediators went into recess but were expected to resume.
Last month the rebels suspended peace talks with the government of President Ernesto Zedillo that had continued on and off for a year and a half.
